The distance at which the asymptotic wall reaches the height of the starting point, which we call the core radius, equals the mean surprisal of the classes that the direction favours, divided by the slope of the wall. Over the parameters of a rectifier backbone, the loss along a line has a kink wherever the activation pattern of a sample changes. Using the dimension theory of semialgebraic sets, we show that, along almost every line, the samples that switch at one point share an irreducible factor of their pre-activation polynomials. Under a coprimality condition, each kink therefore carries the share of one sample among $n$, so creases comparable to the slope do not form. Measurements on ResNet-18 and ResNet-56 trained on CIFAR-10 illustrate both results, with a test that bounds the size of any crease that sampled loss values can hide.

title: Course-Referenced Lateral Control of Trail-Following Convoys: String Stability and Adaptive Feedforward under Load Uncertainty
summary: Vehicles in a convoy can steer along the GNSS trails of the vehicles ahead when lane markings are unavailable, as on snow covered roads. Since each vehicle's tracking error enters the reference of the next, lateral errors can grow along the convoy. This paper presents a course referenced formulation of trail following in arc length, in which each follower takes the direction of its fitted trail as its heading reference. Error propagation then reduces to a single transfer function. We derive a condition under which combining the trails of the leader and the predecessor keeps the errors bounded for any convoy length, and show that following the predecessor alone lets the errors accumulate without bound, even without amplification, on roads that end turned or shifted sideways. Passenger and cargo loads and tire stiffness vary in practice, and we show that they enter the curvature feedforward through a single coefficient, whose mismatch leaves steady offsets on curves. We propose an adaptive law that estimates this coefficient on curves and removes the offsets. Simulations of an eleven vehicle convoy confirm the analysis.

title: Simplify, Agree, Distill: Label-Free Self-Distillation with Stepping Stones
summary: Can a language model teach itself to reason without labels? On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) uses the model as its own teacher, but strengthens that teacher with a ground-truth solution. The natural label-free substitute, voting over the model's attempts, fails precisely on hard problems: attempts disagree, and their most common answer is often wrong. We propose STONE, a label-free alternative that moves agreement to easier related problems. The model writes these stepping stones, keeps those it solves consistently, and shows the teacher their worked solutions, with final answers removed; the student sees only the original problem. No step reads a label, and inference needs no extra context or model calls. Across five math benchmarks, the proposed method achieves the highest average accuracy for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B in thinking mode. Without thinking mode, it gains 13.2 and 22.7 points, 2.5 and 2.7 times the gains of OPSD with ground-truth solutions.

title: STA: A Split Temporal Adversary Method for Evaluating Robustness of Multimodal RL-based Driving Policies
summary: Multimodal reinforcement learning (MRL) offers a promising paradigm for autonomous driving by jointly leveraging complementary sensor observations to learn effective decision-making policies. However, its effectiveness critically depends on temporal alignment across modalities, making temporal inconsistency a fundamental vulnerability. Even subtle misalignment or latency can corrupt fused representations and ultimately lead to decision failures. Existing studies have explored adversarial attacks to induce cross-modal temporal inconsistencies, thereby enabling systematic evaluation of the temporal robustness of MRL policies. However, existing methods remain limited in generality, realism, and adaptivity. To address these limitations, we propose the Split Temporal Adversary (STA), which formulates multimodal temporal attacks as a unified decision process that jointly optimizes attack timing and modality selection under realistic policy-aware and budget-constrained settings. STA includes two mechanisms: a) a unified multimodal temporal perturbation mechanism that delays observations via historical states, removing the need for modality-specific noise; b) a split multimodal adversarial decision mechanism that jointly optimizes attack timing and modality selection through adaptive optimization while leveraging the victim policy's clean actions to identify sensitive decision patterns. We provide a theoretical analysis of the induced distribution shift and a modality selection principle. Experiments in the CARLA simulator show that STA more than doubles the collision rate of the strongest baseline against PPO while using 17.8\% fewer attack attempts, and that it generalizes to a VLM-based driving policy. These results reveal temporal consistency as a critical vulnerability, highlighting temporal robustness as essential for safe autonomous driving.

title: Adaptive Koopman Predictive Control without Persistent Excitation via Matrix Normal Invariant Priors
summary: Finite-dimensional Koopman models are increasingly used in predictive control, but their accuracy remains limited by truncation errors and offline identification data. Adaptive Koopman predictive control promises to address this limitation, but typically requires closed-loop persistent excitation (PE). Since this is difficult to achieve in practice, in this paper we develop an adaptive generalized Koopman (GeKo) predictive controller that does not require PE. To this end, we formulate a recursive matrix regression in fixed lifted coordinates that extends the Kalman filter with back-to-the-prior forgetting to matrix-valued operators and uses a matrix normal invariant prior, centered at the operator identified offline. For any regressor sequence, and thus under any feedback law, we prove that the covariance remains between two multiples of the prior covariance and that the estimation error is input-to-state stable. On an academic example, a differential-drive robot and a power system with plant changes and little excitation, the invariant-prior estimator yields the lowest overall tracking error among the compared estimators and prevents covariance windup.

title: OverclusterDRG: a Deterministic, LP-Free Heuristic for Robust $k$-Center
summary:
The $k$-center problem is a fundamental formulation for metric clustering. However, its min-max objective is highly sensitive to outliers, motivating the Robust $k$-Center (R$k$C) formulation which permits excluding up to $z$ points as outliers.
  Existing algorithms for R$k$C suffer from scalability issues: LP rounding relies on fractional relaxations that scale poorly, known combinatorial approximation algorithms are computationally expensive due to radius guessing, and scalable randomized heuristics require exponential trial multipliers to guarantee success.
  We present OverclusterDRG, a deterministic, LP-free heuristic for R$k$C. The algorithm leverages the theoretical insight of farthest-point oversampling -- adding exactly $z$ extra candidates to the center set to absorb outliers -- followed by a forward-greedy initialization and a $1$-swap local search. Evaluations across real-world datasets show that OverclusterDRG attains a mean approximation ratio of 1.147 against fractional LP lower bounds on the UCI Adult dataset, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in both clustering quality and speed. By avoiding subset-guessing and exponential trial multipliers, it scales smoothly to $n=10^5$ points where LP solvers and theoretical algorithms become intractable.

title: Baryonic Keys and the Inheritance of Crypto-Assets: Revisiting the Tales From the Crypt Protocol
summary: The inheritance of crypto-assets faces a structural obstacle: ownership is the knowledge of a key, so the key either disappears with its owner or has to be shared beforehand. The Tales From the Crypt Protocol (TFCP) addressed one part of the problem, the distributed and privacy-preserving acknowledgment of a death by a blockchain. We revisit it with a new primitive. A \emph{baryonic key} is a physical object from which bits are obtained only through a measurement, are never stored digitally, and which exists in exactly $n$ copies, where $n$ is neither zero nor unbounded. We define the primitive, outline a candidate instantiation based on a replicated micro-fractured relief, and state its limits: digitising a copy is slow and tamper-evident, not impossible. We also outline other uses of the primitive, from post-quantum pre-shared keys to common coins for Byzantine agreement. We then give a threat model for TFCP, review the attack models of the literature that apply to it, and show where it resists and where it does not. We propose TFCP-B, in which decrypting the will requires both a secret shared among registrars and the response of a baryonic key, and in which heirs claim their share through hash commitments, without any prior key or wallet. We detail each change from TFCP to TFCP-B, with its rationale and its price. TFCP-B removes the anonymity loss caused by colluding registrars and blocks several false-alarm attacks. It does not remove the shallow-account attack, remains exposed to transaction censorship during the deliberation period, and introduces new assumptions on custodians and reading devices. The security arguments are informal and the physical figures are design estimates.

title: Probabilistic Power Estimation and MPC-based Scheduling of Construction Electric Vehicles Supported by Mobile Charging Stations
comment: 5 pages, 2 tables; Submitted to IEEE PESGM 2027
summary: The adoption of construction electric vehicles (CEVs) is held back by sparse on-site charging infrastructure, limited mobility, and insufficient knowledge of their power consumption. Mobile charging stations (MCSs) towed between grid connection points and construction sites address the first barrier, yet scheduling them optimally requires an accurate estimate of the CEV power consumption. In this paper, we address these gaps, first, by estimating the power of each subactivity of a representative CEV (a compact electric excavator) based on real-world construction demonstration data. We use Bayesian linear regression to obtain the subactivity power distributions, accounting for their operational uncertainty. Second, we formulate a mixed-integer program that jointly schedules CEV work and charging together with MCS routing, charging, and discharging, optimizing electricity costs, carbon emissions, work completion, and MCS travel. We embed the optimizer in a shrinking-horizon model predictive control (MPC) loop to perform real-time control on the CEV-MCS system. Two MPC variants, one a certainty-equivalent MPC (CE-MPC) controller, and the other a scenario-based MPC (SB-MPC) controller, are compared in closed-loop against an open-loop day-ahead schedule. Realistic simulations show that SB-MPC performs the best, lowering the operating costs by $60.2\%$ relative to the open-loop baseline, and by $23.3\%$ relative to CE-MPC, demonstrating the efficacy of incorporating predictive control with feedback. The code is available at https://github.com/Shubhanflash22/CEV-MCS-MPC-Joint-Scheduling

title: Geometrically Disentangling Concept Learning from the Language Modeling Loss
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Code: https://github.com/YpLarryWang/concept-energy . Pretrained probes and research artifacts: https://huggingface.co/collections/disentangle-concept-learning/concept-energy-neurips-2026
summary: Language models acquire a vast array of concepts and abilities from next-token prediction alone. We introduce an interpretability framework that exposes how this single loss relates to the development of different concepts at different points during pretraining. We propose Concept Energy, a measure of the concept-specific alignment between a concept subspace and the average gradient outer product (AGOP) of the next-token-prediction loss. The concept subspace captures where the concept currently lives in the model's representation; AGOP captures the directions to which the loss is most sensitive. Across 19 checkpoints of Pythia-410M and -1B and 12 lexical, syntactic, and semantic concepts, we find that the first peak in Concept Energy generally occurs at or before the steepest increase in probe decodability. Furthermore, whereas probe performance usually increases monotonically throughout training, Concept Energy is not confined to a single peak; some concepts exhibit sustained or repeated engagement across pretraining, suggesting that concept learning may require continual reinforcement or occur at multiple points. Our results indicate that the loss contributes to concept learning in a myriad of ways that simple probe performance alone cannot reveal.

title: The Cybersecurity Dataset Observatory: Which Data for AI in Cybersecurity?
summary: AI is increasingly used for cybersecurity tasks such as intrusion and malware detection, in enterprise, industrial, vehicular and mobile networks. Its effectiveness depends on data: models need representative network traffic, both to be trained and to be evaluated realistically. Public datasets of cybersecurity network traffic, however, are scattered across laboratory pages, repositories and aggregators, and are continuously released, corrected and withdrawn: 92 of the 234 datasets we catalog were released in 2023 or later. At this pace, surveys that list them are outdated soon after publication, since they describe the field only as it was when they were written. We present the Cybersecurity dataset observatory, a public and continuously updated catalog of cybersecurity datasets based on network traffic. New datasets are added as they are found or submitted, every record is periodically re-checked against its original source, to which it links rather than hosting the data, and every change is recorded in a public change log. This paper documents the first release: we define a traffic-centered scope and a seven-axis taxonomy, and review 234 datasets (204 original captures and 30 derivatives) across 14 domains. The review shows a field that grows quickly but unevenly, where 91 datasets distribute only processed records, a few laboratories produce a large share of the data, and UAV, wireless and V2X networks have little public evidence, while 5G has few real captures. We then relate the catalog to common uses in AI research, outline a procedure for selecting datasets, and discuss benchmark pitfalls and open gaps.

title: Implicit-Reasoning-Enabled Elastic Semantic Communications for AI-Agent Networks
summary: AI-agent networks introduce new communication demands driven by proactive interactions and autonomous task execution. Existing adaptive semantic communication schemes primarily adjust semantic representations and resource configurations within predefined processing scales and capability sets, which may be insufficient for evolving task requirements. To address this gap, we introduce elastic semantic communications (ESC), a task-driven framework that extends semantic adaptation to the runtime execution and participation of task-supporting capabilities. ESC comprises two complementary dimensions: vertical elasticity adjusts the execution intensity of existing capabilities, while horizontal elasticity reconfigures the participating capability set. The framework connects these dimensions through the expected marginal value of additional information and computation. To realize ESC, we propose an implicit-reasoning-enabled device--edge mechanism that supports variable-depth local inference through shared-parameter state updates and edge-side continuation through wireless transfer of intermediate reasoning states. Experiments on Sudoku-Extreme demonstrate that the benefits of additional inference depend on wireless conditions, while task-aware edge invocation can preserve task accuracy with substantially lower state-transfer overhead.

title: Contextual Non-Convex Bandit Optimization with Two-Point Feedback
summary: We study a non-stochastic contextual bandit problem with Lipschitz losses. At every round, the learner observes the context then picks two actions, observes the difference between their losses, and incurs their mean. The aim is to minimize the regret against a generic non-parametric comparator class of policies mapping contexts to actions; for example, Lipschitz policies and Hölder-smooth policies. We show how relying on a hierarchical discretization technique allows us to improve upon the regret rates achievable under one-point feedback, and even recover the full-information rate in some cases; notably, for sufficiently smooth policy classes or low-dimensional instances. Additionally, for Lipschitz policies, we present an algorithm whose per-round computational complexity is only logarithmic in the time horizon.

title: ProcReverser: Multi-Agent Black-Box Microarchitectural Reverse Engineering for Processor Vulnerability Analysis
summary: When processor implementation details are unavailable, black-box microarchitectural reverse engineering helps security researchers identify hardware conditions related to security vulnerabilities. However, this process requires substantial manual effort to design experiments, develop test programs, and analyze results for each processor. We present ProcReverser, a multi-agent system that automates this process. ProcReverser uses execution feedback to improve experimental plans and test programs and identifies microarchitectural properties from measurements. We develop a comprehensive suite of property identification tasks focused on hardware mechanisms relevant to Spectre-class attacks, covering speculative execution, branch prediction, memory dependence, and cache behavior. We evaluate ProcReverser on the XuanTie C910, the gem5 RISC-V O3 CPU model, and the SiFive P550. ProcReverser achieves Pass@1 and Pass@5 scores of 81.3% and 93.8%, respectively, on C910, and 83.0% and 100.0% on gem5 O3. On the SiFive P550, ProcReverser further characterizes microarchitectural properties covered by the proposed task suite. These findings highlight the potential of automated microarchitectural reverse engineering to support processor vulnerability analysis and defense evaluation.

title: On Lie-Algebraic Conditions for Finite-Dimensional Koopman Bilinear Embeddings of Control-Affine Systems
summary: Koopman bilinear representations for control-affine systems have attracted considerable attention. In this paper, we investigate, from a Lie-algebraic perspective, conditions under which a control-affine system admits a finite-dimensional Koopman bilinear embedding. Specifically, we focus on the Lie algebra generated by the drift and control vector fields. First, we show that the finite-dimensionality of the generated Lie algebra is a necessary condition for the existence of a Koopman bilinear embedding. Next, when the generated Lie algebra contains a nonzero nilpotent ideal, we derive a sufficient condition for the existence of such an embedding. Finally, through an example of a quadratic polynomial system, we demonstrate that the finite-dimensionality of the generated Lie algebra imposes strong restrictions on the vector fields, suggesting that exact finite-dimensional Koopman bilinear embeddings may be nongeneric.

title: Bilateral Log-Linear Attention
summary: Sequence models represent past context at different resolutions, using token-level keys and values, fixed-size recurrent states, or hierarchies of compressed summaries. Full attention supports strong associative recall but requires quadratic work during training and prefill and a linearly growing key-value cache during inference. Linear attention and state-space models reduce these costs through fixed-size recurrent memory, but this compression can limit recall. Log-linear attention offers a middle ground by maintaining logarithmically many state matrices. However, its hierarchy favors finer resolution near the current query while compressing earlier context into coarser summaries. To complement this allocation of resolution, we introduce bilateral log-linear attention, which pairs the existing hierarchy with a second hierarchy anchored at the sequence origin. By combining their reads, the two branches provide finer access to both early and recent context while remaining causal. We derive recurrent and chunkwise parallel formulations for the added branch, preserving log-linear training and prefill work, logarithmic decoding work per token, and logarithmic persistent state storage at fixed feature dimensions and chunk size. In multi-query associative recall, this design raises mean overall test accuracy from 76.37% to 96.12% over forward log-linear attention across multiple training seeds. For pretrained language models under approximate parameter matching, it raises the mean score on six selected RULER needle-in-a-haystack tasks from 26.97% to 50.03% at a context length of 6144 tokens. In the same setting, bilateral attention also outperforms forward log-linear attention on seven of eight downstream retrieval tasks, including question answering and information extraction.

title: Optimal Dynamic Fees for L2s: A Vault Approach
summary: Layer 2 (L2) blockchains incur costs when posting data to Layer 1 (L1) and charge users fees intended to recover those costs. We model this mechanism as a *vault*: user fees increase its balance, L1 posting costs reduce it, and surplus and deficit accumulate over time. Forecast-based fees aim to recover posting costs, but forecast errors accumulate in the vault. Returning the vault balance to a target requires feedback on the accumulated error. Treating the vault as a discrete-time control system, we derive in closed form the optimal trade-off between vault tracking and fee smoothness in an idealized benchmark. The optimal rule retains a fraction of the previous fee and corrects in proportion to the current vault error. This fee-memory fraction is the single parameter tracing the entire trade-off frontier. We compare proportional (P), proportional-integral (PI), and Arbitrum-style controllers against this frontier, both analytically and on historical Ethereum fee data. At the fee movement implied by Arbitrum's current parameters, the optimal rule reduces the benchmark tracking error by about one third. Fee memory improves the tracking-smoothness trade-off.

AI.tldr: 研究提出将Layer2费用视为控制问题，推导出最优记忆反馈规则，使费用更好地跟踪成本，实验表明相较Arbitrum可降低约30%追踪误差
AI.motivation: 分析Layer2区块链费用机制并优化其走势
AI.method: 构建情仓模型，将交易费视为控制系统，推导封闭式最优反馈规则，并与P、PI、Arbitrum控制器比较
AI.result: 最优规则保留上一费的一定比例并按当时误差校正，三分之一跟踪误差下降；记忆因子显著提升平滑-跟踪权衡
AI.conclusion: 在L2费用设计中加入记忆反馈可显著改善费用对成本收支的自适应性，为协议调优提供理论依据

title: Estimation of jam density and saturation flow at signalized intersections using only low penetration rate connected vehicle GNSS trajectories: Case study using actual data in Tokyo
comment: Preprint ("Submitted Manuscript'') accepted by International Journal of Intelligent Transportation Systems Research.\\ First submission: 2026-05-29. Accepted: 2026-10-16
summary: The jam density and saturation flow at a signalized intersection are basic inputs to traffic signal management schemes that use connected vehicle (CV) trajectory data. However, methods for estimating the jam density itself from low penetration rate CV trajectories have received little attention. Although a few theoretical methods have been proposed, their application is very limited and it is not clear whether those parameters can be estimated using actual CV data, especially with low penetration rates. This paper analyze such methods, in which the jam density and saturation flow are estimated from long-term historical distribution of low penetration rate CV stop positions accumulated over many signal cycles. The methods are evaluated using actual CV trajectory data collected at three signalized intersections in Tokyo for six months, with a penetration rate on the order of 1--3%. The estimators mostly agree on a jam spacing close to 8~m at the sites at which the queueing pattern is well developed, and the saturation flow estimates lie within roughly 10% of an independent video-based reference at those sites. Furthermore, quantitative criteria for self-evaluation of reliability of the estimates are proposed.

title: Large language models as oncology world models
comment: 63 pages (main text 35, Supplementary Information 28), 6 figures, 9 Extended Data figures. Code: https://github.com/julienvibert/llm-oncology-world-models. Data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24137512
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can synthesize cancer patient cases, but their internal representation of oncology, or world model, has not been explored systematically. By only specifying tumor type, we show that LLMs tend to generate similar patients per cancer, with on average 81.0% to 93.2% of a cancer's patients sharing the most frequent value of each baseline feature. By systematically varying patient features in 12 clinical scenarios, we show that they follow biomarker and treatment logic in 29 of 36 model-scenario assessments, against 1 of 12 when previous treatment or frailty matters. Continuing real patient trajectories, an LLM predicted 89.9% 12-month survival, and 79.2% with similar patients as examples, against 72.2% observed. To represent these trajectories, we developed the Clinical State Space, a dynamic representation framework that we also applied to real patients. Despite the limits we show, improved world models may support digital twins, which our framework can evaluate.

title: Scenario-Based Risk Certificates for Multi-Property Vulnerability Discovery in Parametric MDPs
summary: Safety-critical systems such as network protocols and distributed algorithms depend on environmental parameters whose exact values are uncertain. Parametric Markov decision processes (pMDPs) model such systems by making transition probabilities symbolic functions of the parameters. For a single quantitative requirement, parametric verification asks which parameter valuations satisfy the requirement. In practice, however, engineers often monitor several safety and performance requirements at once, and one valuation may make several requirements vulnerable simultaneously. In this paper we study multi-property vulnerability discovery under requirement-wise semantics: given a pMDP and M quantitative requirements, we construct candidate regions of the parameter space that may contain violations, and study budgets for random testing under a specified parameter distribution. To solve this, we adopt a two-layered approach in which the scenario-approximation layer provides PAC guarantees on identifying conservative vulnerability regions for each requirement while the testing layer treats random parameter exploration as coverage of overlapping regions and yields a stopping certificate computed from the marginal region masses alone; a composition theorem then bounds the expected non-discovery score by the scenario approximation error plus the testing risk from the two layers. For confirmed discoveries, candidate hits are checked by model checking and budgets use independently certified discovery probabilities. Experiment evaluate these certificates using empirical surrogates and independent confidence bounds.

title: Time-Varying Coverage via Diffeomorphic Coverage Control
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, accepted into Conference on Decision and Control 2026
summary: This paper addresses a structured class of time-varying coverage control in which region-density evolution is parameterised by a time-varying diffeomorphism acting on a static region-density pair. We refer to this setting as diffeomorphic coverage control. Such trajectories arise naturally in mass-conserving transport flows and in density-driven formation control. We propose decentralised diffeomorphic coverage controllers for both continuous- and discrete-time dynamics that achieve time-varying coverage by solving a related time-invariant coverage problem in a nominal domain. The resulting controllers are asymptotically stable with respect to a variant of a popular coverage metric under corresponding time-varying regions and densities. Further analysis shows that diffeomorphic coverage corresponds to a time-varying non-uniform coverage problem over a non-Euclidean metric. Simulations demonstrate effectiveness of the proposed control strategy under affine diffeomorphisms in a formation control task, achieving performance comparable to a popular centralised coverage control law. Coverage performance is also demonstrated under non-affine diffeomorphisms.

title: Revealing the Biases of Large Language Models By Inferring Prior Distributions
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been known to exhibit a wide range of social biases including name-nationality associations, occupation-gender associations and racial stereotypes. Existing approaches to evaluating these biases typically involve measuring surface-level behavior where a model is fed a dataset of prompts and its outputs are scored relative to ground-truth answers. Inspired by prior elicitation in cognitive science, we propose a different perspective that reconstructs latent bias as a prior underlying the model's behavior. We formulate the problem as a Bayesian inverse problem where, given prompt-response observations on a bias benchmark dataset, we infer a low-dimensional latent distribution that summarizes the model's stereotyping tendencies. This paper develops the mathematical foundation, a practical reconstruction algorithm, and experiments using the Bias Benchmark for QA (BBQ) benchmark to infer the prior distributions of LLMs over responses in ambiguous social contexts.

title: AudioTrace: File-Level Membership Detection for Audio Large Language Models
summary:
Significant privacy and copyright concerns are raised by the use of publicly available audio recordings to train audio large language models (LLMs), yet effective auditing methods remain limited. Existing membership inference attacks typically assume knowledge of complete training examples, including their associated textual supervision. In practice, however, audio recordings may be paired with privately generated transcripts, captions, or question-answer pairs that are unavailable to owners of the recordings. This motivates audio-file-level membership inference, which determines whether a recording was used for training without assuming knowledge of its training tasks and annotations. This paper provides the first systematic investigation of this challenge and introduces AudioTraceBench, a controlled benchmark comprising 1,285 audio recordings with explicit fine-tuning membership labels. Evaluations across three audio LLMs show that existing text- and video-based membership inference methods adapted to audio perform close to random guessing.
  To address this challenge, AudioTrace is proposed, where audio-conditioned proxy questions are generated using the target model, and membership evidence is extracted from its responses and aggregated at the recording level. Consistent improvements over existing baselines are observed, with AUROC reaching 0.60 and increasing further under increased fine-tuning exposure or adaptation capacity. Further experiments were conducted to examine the factors influencing membership signals for audio-file-level detection. These findings establish audio-file-level membership inference as a distinct and practically important auditing challenge, with AudioTrace providing an effective initial approach to this challenge.

title: Compositional Data-Driven Small-Signal Stability Assessment of Power Systems via Output Differential Passivity
summary: This paper proposes a compositional data-driven small-signal stability assessment framework for interconnected power systems based on output differential passivity (ODP). Without requiring explicit device models, local ODP matrices and scalar indices are estimated directly from measurement trajectories. When internal states are available, trajectory-based linear matrix inequalities (LMIs) are constructed from input-state measurements to estimate the local ODP matrices and scalar indices. When internal states are unavailable, an extended-state representation is constructed from input-output measurements, enabling the same assessment using only external signals. The estimated ODP matrices are combined with the network coupling matrix for compositional assessment of power system stability, while their scalar indices enable decentralized assessment. To address the computational and numerical challenges of trajectory-based LMIs, we introduce right-inverse whitening (RIW) to remove redundant behavioral coordinates and improve computational efficiency, and apply instrumental-variable (IV) preprocessing to alleviate numerical ill-conditioning and mitigate noise effects. Case studies on a modified IEEE 39-bus power system show that ambient measurements satisfy the required informativity conditions and that both formulations yield estimates close to model-based references under the tested noise levels. The reusable local ODP estimates also enable modular stability reassessment after controller updates.

title: AdaMenu: Query-Adaptive Menus for Decision Models over Large Label Spaces
summary: Decision models such as Jev return probabilities over caller-defined options and are increasingly used for classification. Large label spaces challenge both accuracy and scalability: larger menus can impair decisions, increase input costs, and exceed option limits. Hierarchical classification reduces menu size but introduces serial calls and error propagation. We propose AdaMenu, which builds a compact candidate menu from retrieved labeled examples and makes a single decision-model request. Its candidate labels adapt to the query, and its default setting also adjusts menu size using aggregated retrieval scores. We evaluate AdaMenu with open and closed decision models on four label sets containing up to 1,016 labels. It outperforms TypeSafe's beam-search baseline on all 16 model and label-set pairs where both methods run, improving accuracy by 16.6-34.3 percentage points. Relative to the full menu on the three smaller label sets, accuracy differences range from -0.5 to +7.2 percentage points, while input token usage falls by factors of 3.2-22.9. AdaMenu also runs when option limits exclude the full menu, including settings where the hierarchical baseline is unavailable.

title: Exposure and remediation in the French maritime sector: a passive measurement of 129 organisations
comment: 5 pages, 5 tables. Also deposited on Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.24279346
summary: Maritime transport and ports are essential entities under the EU NIS2 directive, but there is little public data on the external exposure of the sector in France. In March 2026, after physical attacks on Western interests in the Middle East raised the risk of cyber retaliation against French maritime operators, we assessed the internet-facing attack surface of 129 organisations: 103 French companies and 26 international operators active in French waters. The March assessment was passive. It used DNS and email-authentication records, TLS certificates, search-engine indexing, archived pages, public JavaScript, cloud storage naming and third-party internet-scan data (Shodan), with no connection attempt beyond ordinary public web requests. After manual verification we retained 475 findings, 3.7 per organisation. 46% of organisations had at least one high or critical finding and 11% at least one critical finding, including exposed databases, unpatched services with known CVEs, an exposed credentials file, publicly listed cloud buckets and a subdomain open to takeover. The most common gap was email spoofing protection, with no enforced DMARC policy at 60% of organisations. French companies fared worse than international operators (49% vs 35% at high or critical risk; 4.0 vs 2.3 findings per organisation). Between 2 and 18 March 2026, individual reports were sent for 43 of the audited domains. We rescanned 123 organisations in November 2026. Among March critical and high findings that could be rechecked, 52% were gone for organisations that had received a report and 54% for those that had not, so private email disclosure had no measurable effect on remediation. Results are aggregated and anonymised.

title: Social Welfare and Equilibrium in Distributed Microgrid Prosumer Coordination Under a Mixed Competitive-Cooperative Setting
comment: This paper is submitted to IEEE transactions on control of network systems
summary: Price-based distributed prosumer coordination in distribution networks is fundamentally challenging when the aggregator pursues grid-level goals that couple prosumers' decisions, because the Lagrangian fails to separate and nodal prices are undefined under conventional dual decomposition. This paper develops a novel method that embeds mixed competitive-cooperative objectives exactly into prices, which are split into energy, congestion, and grid-objective components, closing the gap between the social welfare optimum and the competitive equilibrium. To compute the equilibrium, a distributed optimization algorithm is developed based on the projected Arrow-Hurwicz-Uzawa scheme. Explicit step-size rules are developed for the algorithm to guarantee $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{L})$ and $\mathcal{O}(1/L)$ ergodic convergence rates. Simulations on an IEEE 33-bus feeder that is connected to prosumers and electric vehicle fleets validate the accuracy and efficacy of the proposed methods.

title: Advancing the Calibration-Compute Frontier of LLM Classifiers via Asymmetric Duos
summary: The importance of reliable uncertainty estimation in large language models (LLMs) has become increasingly pronounced, yet modern models remain poorly calibrated and frequently overconfident. In this study, we address this by proposing an efficient method for LLM classifier calibration using the Asymmetric Duos framework. Our approach combines a strong base model with a smaller sidekick model via logit-space fusion, utilizing global scaling parameters optimized on a validation set. Across diverse benchmarks, this Asymmetric LLM Duo consistently achieves best or second-best performance on expected calibration error and negative log-likelihood, without degrading predictive accuracy. More importantly, these gains are realized at a fraction of the computational cost of more complex baselines, placing our method on the calibration-compute Pareto frontier. We further demonstrate that our method acts orthogonal to various established calibration-aware techniques, meaning it can be easily combined with them to consistently boost their performance. Finally, our analysis of the logit-space behavior illustrates how asymmetric fusion successfully mitigates base model overconfidence. Overall, our findings demonstrate that the benefits of an asymmetric fusion successfully transfer to the language domain, providing a simple, highly cost-efficient approach to improving uncertainty estimation in LLM classifiers.

title: PQC Migration: End-to-End Performance Profiling of Post Quantum Cryptographic Algorithms in mTLS
summary: Emerging quantum computers threaten to break the classical key exchange algorithms. To safeguard against these threats, migration to new quantum-safe algorithms is underway and expected to be expedited. Though resistant to attacks, the quantum safe algorithms may impact the real-world performance due to their large key lengths. In this work, we analyze the end-to-end performance of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol with the post-quantum (PQ) and hybrid cryptographic algorithms standardized by NIST. We develop a test setup to evaluate the performance of TLS connections between a client and a server under various network conditions. We focus on the impact of the new algorithms on the speed (throughput, connection time) and sustainability (energy, CPU cycles) of TLS 1.3. Our analysis demonstrates that the standardized post-quantum algorithms do not introduce any measurable performance degradations in TLS 1.3, despite their larger key lengths. However, hybrid algorithms introduce noticeable performance degradation, which becomes increasingly pronounced under adverse network conditions. Our analysis suggests that migration to hybrid algorithms should be ``network condition aware'' as poor network conditions can severely degrade performance in TLS 1.3. We provide anonymised link to the code and a web interface to analyse performance of various combination of algorithms.

title: Tensor-Algebraic Framework for Nonlinear Control: Spectral Stability Analysis and Controller Design of Polynomial Systems
summary: Matrices provide an algebraic foundation for systems and control, whereas an analogous tensor-based framework for general nonhomogeneous polynomial dynamics is still lacking. This paper addresses this gap by developing a tensor-algebraic framework that connects tensor structure, spectral properties, Lyapunov stability, and controller synthesis. We first establish stability conditions based on positive-definite, copositive, and P-tensors for homogeneous and nonhomogeneous polynomial systems. We then introduce an extended tensor-eigenvalue problem (ETEP) for general multivariate polynomials, yielding a spectral-variational characterization of positivity through one interior and two boundary spectral quantities, and consequently a stability test for polynomial vector fields. For controller synthesis, we develop an unfolding-based U-eigenvalue relaxation that combines a positive-definite anchor with a near-positive-semidefinite higher-order part, leading to a convex semidefinite program. The conservatism of the relaxation is explicitly characterized, and an explicit guaranteed domain-of-attraction bound is derived. Numerical examples demonstrate positivity certification beyond direct SOS representations and substantially lower computation time than SOS-based synthesis in the considered example. These results establish a systematic tensor-spectral methodology for the analysis and control of polynomial systems with higher-order interactions.

title: Taking Time Out of TOCTOU: From Race Reproduction to Security Discovery
summary: Time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) races are hard to reproduce and lost races can make vulnerable programs look fixed. We present Chronos, a framework that separates intervention timing from verdict evidence and builds reusable one-trial security regression oracles from declared races for deterministic reproduction, commit bisection and CI. Race Specifications compose reusable hold engines, actions, observers and outcome rules. When the declared hold is reached and the attack completes while held, Chronos orders it before the use under blocking and interference assumptions. Chronos uses seccomp notifications to enforce declared hold-attack-release ordering at syscall boundaries on stock Linux; ptrace and a KVM guest gate provide holds at userspace and kernel instruction sites. One decision procedure labels every mechanism's runs: fixed requires positive, case-specific evidence of preservation, justified refusal, omission under checked coverage, or a declared rule; missing or contradictory required evidence remains indeterminate. On known-vulnerable builds, effect-only checkers made over 800 false-fixed classifications in failed-intervention trials; Chronos made none. All 17 syscall-held cases and four of six instruction-held cases had vulnerable and fixed labels. Two kernel cases remain one-sided. All 27 historical bisections recovered the expected boundaries. For runc's masked-path bisection with one victim per launch, fixed retry and Git Bayesect took medians of 475 and 398 natural launches; Chronos used seven held trials including endpoint checks. Since a label means the same however a fix is written, we also ran the specifications and attack variants on releases, distribution packages and other runtimes. There, Chronos helped us uncover three issues: incomplete fixes in chrony and rpm, and a Debian rpm package its tracker listed as fixed.

title: Distribution-Free Probabilistic Environmental Control Barrier Functions with Application to Adaptive Cruise Control
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures. Submitted to the 2027 American Control Conference (ACC)
summary: Safety control under environmental uncertainty is challenging when the uncertainty distribution is unknown and reliable support bounds are unavailable. This paper introduces CPP-ECBF, a distribution-free approach that combines conformal predictive programming with probabilistic environmental control barrier functions. For separable environmental safety functions and i.i.d. uncertainty, CPP-ECBF converts the probabilistic safety condition into a sample-based deterministic control constraint that provides finite-horizon safety with prescribed probability $1-ε$ and calibration confidence $1-\tildeβ$. For adaptive cruise control, an offline conformal uncertainty bound yields an explicit linear upper bound on the ego-vehicle acceleration, which is enforced by a quadratic-programming safety filter. In 10,000 Monte Carlo trials, 99.97% of trials satisfied the finite-horizon safety criterion, exceeding the prescribed confidence of 85%. Moreover, CPP-ECBF reduced the conservatism of worst-case robust enforcement, increasing the admissible acceleration upper limit by $5.90\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ on average.

title: The Critic Can Hurt: On the Safety of Critics in LLM-Guided AutoML Search
summary: LLM critics increasingly steer iterative search in agentic AutoML, prompt optimization, and self-refinement--evaluated for whether they help, but rarely for whether they can hurt. We isolate the critic's marginal effect through a four-arm audit and characterize the loop's tolerance through controlled fault injection. We show a naive 8B critic drives search below the no-critic random-search floor on 7 of 8 tabular datasets, losing up to 0.245 AUC in the worst case; the magnitude varies strongly with dataset, frontier, and budget. When: stronger critics attenuate the loss on the evaluated suite, without establishing a universal capability threshold. Why: controlled fault injection shows that non-directional errors are nearly costless under best-so-far search, whereas directional errors consume finite search opportunities; an idealized effective-sample calculation yields a necessary condition, $q(m-1) > β$, not a deployment certificate. How: a simple observable validation gate and a learned detector can reduce realized loss, but neither is guaranteed to preserve the full-budget no-critic baseline. We will release CRITFAULT, to our knowledge the first benchmark for detecting harmful critic feedback in AutoML. A critic is not a free addition: audit before trusting, and gate when capability or verification is insufficient.

title: Verifiable Random Sampling of Private Data Without a Trusted Single Party
summary:
Problem: When a party supports claims about a private dataset by disclosing a sample, auditors cannot tell whether it was drawn at random or "cherry-picked" to hide flaws in the rest of the data.
  Solution: The data holder commits to the hashes of every item in its dataset and registers the commitment with independent servers. Selection then waits on a decentralized randomness beacon: a network that jointly emits a fresh random value every few seconds, outside the control of the data holder and the auditors. The value emitted two beacon rounds after the commitment picks the sample. Each server returns a signed receipt, so anyone can later check that the revealed sample is exactly the one that value prescribes. Selection from the committed set stays unbiased as long as the beacon's threshold holds and one required server is honest, and a pre-agreed name, checked with the servers, stops repeated or abandoned draws. We call this protocol NoCherry.
  Applications: Any audit that spot-checks a private corpus: private AI benchmarks and held-out test sets, dataset quality claims, code and security audits, test-fairness review, vulnerability handling, and compliance sampling. Auditors need not trust the data holder to hand over a representative sample of the committed data, since the protocol proves it, and data holders need not expose their entire dataset.

title: Koopman Temporal Logic and Model Predictive Control of Nonlinear Systems: A Demonstration in AC-DC Power Conversion
summary: This paper proposes a novel temporal logic, which we call Koopman Temporal Logic (KTL), towards a formal method in which Koopman operator theory provides a mathematical way to verify and control systems with nonlinear dynamics. We first review signal temporal logic and then introduce KTL, including its syntax, Boolean semantics, and quantitative semantics. Next, we propose a formulation of Model Predictive Control (MPC) from a control specification described by KTL. Effectiveness and computational efficiency of the proposed MPC formulation are evaluated by applying it to a reliable design of AC-DC power conversion.

title: Understanding the Role of Reasoning Data in Pretraining
summary: Reasoning data expose models to multi-step reasoning, but reasoning traces may cover only a subset of the available facts. How should pretraining balance atomic facts with reasoning traces? We study this question by constructing a setting in which every fact provides an atomic training signal, while only a subset appears in reasoning supervision, enabling us to measure generalization to transitions observed atomically but never used in training traces. For a linear transformer, we derive the weight assigned to atomic training signals that minimizes held-transition squared error and show that its leading-order optimum increases with reasoning-chain length and decreases with the fraction of facts held out from reasoning traces. These trends persist in a full transformer layer with an MLP, softmax attention, and cross-entropy loss. We further validate the role of reasoning complexity and data coverage in two natural-language settings: controlled multi-hop reasoning and mathematical pretraining. Together, our results provide a principled view of how reasoning-chain structure and data coverage should shape the allocation of training data during pretraining.

title: TRIAGE-CPG: A Cross-Model Study of Budgeted Static Malware Triage with Large Language Models
comment: Code and artifacts available here: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22771897
summary: When triaging unknown binaries, security analysts must decide which samples to clear as benign, flag as malicious, or escalate for deeper analysis. Large Language Models (LLMs) could support these decisions by interpreting decompiled code, but a binary can contain hundreds or thousands of functions, making exhaustive LLM analysis impractical. We study how current LLMs behave when static triage is formulated as budgeted evidence acquisition: which functions they inspect and how they trade off benign clearance, malware detection, and escalation. To enable a controlled comparison, we implement TRIAGE-CPG, a fixed pipeline over a code property graph (CPG) of a decompiled binary. An LLM-free heuristic selects seed functions, an agent expands the resulting evidence dossier under a fixed budget, and a reporting stage produces a benign, suspicious, or malicious verdict together with a behavioral report. We evaluate eight closed-source and open-weight models on 1,000 Windows PE binaries, using a 600-sample test split and the same zero-shot protocol for every model. We assess the ternary verdicts under both a strict binary reading and triage balanced accuracy (tBA), which credits malware that is flagged or escalated and benign samples only when cleared. After analyzing about 40 of a mean 1,000 functions per binary, the highest-scoring model reaches a strict balanced accuracy of 0.805 and a tBA of 0.855, flagging 65% of malware, escalating another 12%, and clearing 94% of benign samples. The models implement different triage policies: high-specificity models produce small, malware-rich escalation queues, whereas recall-oriented models escalate or flag much more broadly. Both closed-source and open-weight models appear across this spectrum. Our results identify no universal deployment configuration: model choice itself determines the clear/flag/escalate trade-off under limited static evidence.

title: NL2RCtrl: Risk-Controlled Controller Synthesis from Natural Language Requirements
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled the translation of natural language (NL) requirements into linear temporal logic (LTL) specifications, facilitating controller synthesis for cyber-physical systems (CPSs). However, the reliability of such translations remains a concern in safety-critical applications, particularly when NL requirements are ambiguous. This paper proposes a framework based on Conformal Risk Control (CRC) to provide a statistical guarantee on the risk of issuing a controller that violates the user's intended requirement. Rather than requiring semantic equivalence between the generated and intended specifications, the proposed approach considers language inclusion, a sufficient condition for ensuring that the traces of a controller synthesized for the generated specification satisfy the intended requirement. To account for ambiguity, the LLM is queried multiple times, and the resulting LTL specifications are grouped into semantic equivalence classes and ranked by their frequency of occurrence. Given a prescribed risk level, CRC selects how many of the top-ranked equivalence classes to combine into a single LTL specification, such that the probability of issuing a controller that violates the intended requirement is bounded by that level. A controller is then synthesized for the resulting specification, or the framework abstains. Experiments on a vehicle navigation case study evaluate the proposed approach.

title: A Fast Algorithm for the Familywise Loss
summary: The familywise (FW) loss for multiclass classification, introduced by Duchi, Ruan, and Khosravi, achieves universal equivalence to the 0-1 loss, and thus has stronger theoretical properties than cross entropy (CE). Prior work, however, left open whether FW is as computationally efficient as CE. First, on the theoretical side, we prove that the FW gradient can be computed in $O(K)$ time, where $K$ is the number of classes. Second, on the practical side, we develop optimized kernels for computing the forward and backward passes of FW which outperform CE in terms of speed on both CPU and GPU.

title: A counterexample to the soundness of the Flowering IOPP for codes on graphs
summary: The Flowering protocol of Delavenne, Medevielle and Roussel (ISIT 2025, arXiv:2501.14337) and its generalization by Delavenne and Lallemand (CANS 2025, arXiv:2508.10510) are Interactive Oracle Proofs of Proximity (IOPPs) for codes on graphs with Reed-Solomon local codes. Similarly to FRI for Reed-Solomon codes, the graph is recursively cut into isomorphic subgraphs and the word is folded along the cuts. We show that the soundness claims of both papers are false. The commit soundness proofs identify the vertex distance of a word to the code with the fraction of its unsatisfied local constraints, while only one inequality holds, in the wrong direction. We furthermore give an explicit counterexample.

title: Co-simulation-Based Safety-Assessment of Black-Box Maritime Cyber-Physical Systems
summary: Modern maritime cyber-physical systems consist of tightly interconnected subsystems ranging from multiple engineering domains, making exhaustive safety verification impractical. Simulation-based testing offers a scalable alternative, while co-simulation enables heterogeneous subsystem models, potentially developed by different stakeholders, to be integrated without requiring access to their internal implementations. Adaptive Stress-Testing further improves testing efficiency by formulating failure discovery as a sequential decision-making problem, guiding the search toward the most likely failure scenarios, and giving the counter safety examples using reinforcement learning. However, black-box co-simulation may provide only partial access to the system state required by conventional Markov decision process formulations. To address this limitation, we proposed Event-Based Adaptive Stress-Testing version 2, a co-simulation-based safety-assessment method formulated as a partially observable Markov decision process. This method employs Recurrent Proximal Policy Optimization to exploit observation histories when selecting adversarial actions. The method is evaluated on a ship-in-transit operation in which a collision-avoidance system is stress-tested against multi-adversarial target ships. An extended Intermediate Waypoint Sampling mechanism enables independent multi-adversary trajectory control and supports the generation of realistic collision-inducing scenarios. The experiment demonstrate that the learned stress-testing policy generalizes across different encounter cases, can be further improved through continued training, and can be made effective when the collision- avoidance system under test is replaced by another version. These results demonstrate the method's potential for scalable black-box safety assessment of complex maritime cyber-physical systems.

title: Nahual: A Sequence Model for Language and Atoms
summary: Generative models play a rapidly growing role in the design and simulation of molecules. The most widely used applications of generative models are in large language models (LLMs), owing to the natural flexibility of language for specifying and answering queries. However, generalist LLMs do not effectively handle large sets of 3D coordinates, whereas specialist generative models of 3D molecules cannot reach the controllability afforded by language. To bridge these capabilities, we propose Nahual, a decoder-only autoregressive diffusion model for any sequence of text and 3D molecules. To enable expressive autoregression on continuous coordinates, we propose next-token diffusion, whereby a causal transformer denoises each token while attending to the clean tokens before it, without increasing context size. We train Nahual on a curated set of twelve 3D chemistry tasks ranging from microsolvation to molecular conformer search to adsorption on metal surfaces, with associated evaluation metrics and baselines. The result is a single set of end-to-end-trained weights that simultaneously performs all tasks and surpasses state-of-the-art models specialized for crystal structure prediction and property-conditional molecule generation. Our results demonstrate the viability of scaling generalist decoder-only models for native multimodal understanding and generation across language and chemistry. Code is available at https://github.com/the-matter-lab/nahual.

title: Expertise capture in workplace AI
summary: AI assistants are becoming part of how knowledge workers think and perform, accumulating the prompts, exemplars, memory and interaction histories that encode a worker's professional judgment. This infrastructure typically runs under employer or platform control. We name the resulting process expertise capture, the absorption of worker-applied knowledge and judgment into AI resources under organizational control. We develop a framework of contribution forms, technical residences and transformation families, and show that how far a contribution can be attributed, separated and revoked depends on where it resides and how it has been transformed, properties fixed by system design long before any dispute arises. When a worker departs, the organization retains a capability shaped by their judgment while the worker loses access to it, and the asymmetry compounds as contributions move from inspectable artifacts into derivatives, learned components and successor systems. We outline three measures, write-time provenance, extraction of separable contributions and an executable exit procedure, that make an agreed allocation technically performable, and make explicit what cannot be separated at all.

title: Universal Quantizer Design for Identification of Systems with Memory
summary: In system identification from quantized observations, the quantizer determines how much information about the parameters the observations retain, and hence the achievable estimation accuracy. Quantizer design can be guided by the Fisher information matrix (FIM), which assesses the parameter information retained by candidate quantizers. Existing methods, however, typically rely on closed-form expressions of the FIM. This paper proposes a universal quantizer design method for general systems with memory. Its core is a universal FIM estimator that evaluates the information per bit from simulated trajectories, and the thresholds are designed by maximizing the estimated criterion under a bit budget. For unknown parameters, the design is implemented through a two-stage procedure. Numerical studies on a quantized ARX system yield designs close to the reference optimum, while a nonlinear cascaded-tanks example reduces the identification error by about 50% relative to a single median threshold.

title: DynaDFlash: Dynamic Feature Projection for Block Diffusion Speculators
comment: Code and trained models available at https://github.com/midas-llm-research/DynaDFlash
summary: DFlash trains a parallel draft model on hidden features from its target model. Inspired by the previous work of DFlare that introduced per layer combinations of target hidden states, we test whether context dependent weighting of these states helps improve acceptance length of block diffusion speculators. We trained both a DFlash baseline for the Qwen 3 of block size 16, and a dynamic model that computes gates for each layer to affect the magnitude of hidden features before projection. While mean acceptance length between the dynamic model and the DFlash baseline didn't significantly differ, we notice that the dynamic model excels for drafting in the context of math. In an evaluation of 700 prompts from the MetaMathQA and Orca-Math datasets, the mean accepted length improves by 5%. We also found this lead to a 4.1% higher throughput for a subset of the same dataset in the context of speculative decoding.

title: RESILAGENT: A Three-Pillar Architecture for Cyber-Physical Resilience in Electrical Power and Energy Systems
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Cyber Security and Resilience (IEEE CSR 2026)
summary: Electrical Power and Energy Systems face hybrid threats that combine cyber intrusions, physical sabotage and climate-driven stress, and routinely outpace today's siloed monitoring stacks. We present RESILAGENT, a concept architecture organised around three operational pillars, Sensing & Data Intelligence, Resilience Analytics & Reporting, and Incident Response & Recovery, mediated by a Cloud-based Orchestrator and exercised through a closed Detect-Simulate-Decide-Sign loop. The framework fuses agentic artificial intelligence and multimodal large language models for cross-modal detection, real-time digital twins for what-if simulation, and a permissioned blockchain anchor for tamper-evident threat intelligence and CER/NIS2-aligned evidence. We instantiate it on two scenarios, a transmission operator under coordinated cyber compromise, sabotage and heatwave, and a distribution operator under a supply-chain compromise during a storm, and report an IEEE-bus micro-benchmark that quantifies each pillar through false-data-injection attack detection, cyber-physical fusion lift, N-1 contingency screening and anchor cost.

title: Comfort as a Constraint or as a Cost in Reinforcement Learning and Model Predictive Building Control
summary: A building controller that keeps a zone within comfort bounds at minimum energy can treat the bounds as a soft constraint, by adding the weighted violation to its cost, or as a hard constraint. We analyze the effect of the hard and the soft formulation of the same problem and isolate the effect of the formulation from the effect of the algorithm. To this end, we measure the difference in energy use between the two formulations on the BOPTEST bestest_hydronic_heat_pump case, in model predictive control (MPC) and in reinforcement learning (RL). The soft formulations are a weighted MPC and weighted SAC and DDPG learners, each at twelve weights. The hard formulations are an MPC with an exact penalty and the Lagrangian learners SAC-Lagrangian and primal-dual DDPG. We find that the hard formulations use more energy than the soft formulations at the largest weight, but violate the comfort bounds less. For a large weight, the soft formulation approaches the behavior of the hard formulation. The frontiers of the energy-comfort trade-off of the three weighted controllers lie close to each other, and the weight selects an operating point on this frontier. Under the soft formulation, the three algorithms reach very similar operating points, although at somewhat different weights. For this HVAC problem, the formulation and the weight thus affect the energy use more than the choice of algorithm.

title: Knowledge-Guided Local-to-Global Anomaly Learning for Longitudinal Medication Trajectories
summary: Detecting suspicious deviations in longitudinal medication trajectories requires distinguishing knowledge-consistent treatment variations from anomalous changes and linking local deviations to account-level decisions. We propose a knowledge-guided local-to-global (L2G) anomaly learning framework that addresses both challenges. It constructs proxy supervision at three granularities: medication occurrences, treatment episodes, and contiguous visit segments. Knowledge-consistent medication and episode replacements provide plausible negatives, while cross-category and cross-account perturbations provide suspicious proxies. A medication-multiset encoder and causal visit-sequence encoder feed a shared scoring head that produces visit-level anomaly logits. Top-\(α\) aggregation derives account-level scores from these logits, while account-level classification and class-balanced visit-localization objectives jointly optimize the same visit-level evidence. Experiments on two city cohorts compare L2G with native and proxy-adapted anomaly methods. On City-A, L2G outperforms the strongest comparators. Cross-city results show more consistent gains in localization than in account-level detection.

title: Detection-Efficient Watermarking for Vision--Language Agents via Risk-Constrained Strength Allocation
summary: Vision--language agents generate descriptions, decisions, and instructions that may be reused by users, downstream agents, and automated workflows, creating a need for provenance mechanisms that support content authenticity and post-deployment auditing without unnecessarily degrading response quality. We present a risk-aware semantic watermarking framework that combines predictive uncertainty with a zero-shot multimodal relevance-risk proxy to allocate watermark strength during decoding. A single risk penalty $λ$ exposes a continuous operating frontier, allowing deployment-time selection of a detection--quality trade-off without model retraining. At a selected operating point, mean watermark strength is reduced by approximately 59.4\% relative to fixed-strength watermarking, while perplexity change falls from 0.3634 to 0.1689 and clean/paraphrased ROC-AUC reaches 0.9552/0.9459. A matched-strength analysis shows that this advantage reflects the allocation policy rather than lower average intervention: at comparable mean strength, risk-constrained allocation achieves substantially higher ROC-AUC than fixed, entropy-only, and criticality-only policies, identifying it as detection-efficient rather than quality-dominant. We further show that threshold calibration on finite samples produces substantial false-positive-rate drift, motivating calibration variance reporting as standard practice for auditable provenance.

title: Joint Learning of Control Lyapunov Functions and Controllers via Stable-by-Design Surrogates
summary: Training and verifying neural network-based control Lyapunov functions (CLFs) can be computationally demanding. To address this challenge, we propose a framework that jointly learns a CLF and a stabilizing controller using structured neural networks and a projection-based parameterization. Specifically, we employ Polyak-Lojasiewicz networks (PLNets), which parameterize nonconvex, positive-definite CLF candidates, and construct a stable-by-design surrogate of the closed-loop dynamics that satisfies the Lyapunov decrease condition by construction. The controller combines linear state feedback with a higher-order correction term resembling Sontag's universal formula and is trained to align the resulting closed-loop dynamics with the stable-by-design surrogate. Unlike classical approaches based on Sontag's formula, our framework does not require a known CLF; instead, it learns the CLF and controller simultaneously. We establish local and global stability guarantees for the learned controller and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach through numerical examples.

title: Empowering Masked Diffusion Models to Self-Correct with Leave-One-Out Transformers
summary: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for language modeling, enabling parallel token generation with competitive performance. Yet standard MDMs suffer from two fundamental limitations: (1) inability to revise tokens, and (2) sparse training signal. We revisit hollow transformers, which address both limitations by predicting each token from its surrounding context, independently of the input at that position. We introduce the Leave-One-Out Transformer (LOOT), a more efficient and expressive architecture that advances hollow transformers through two complementary advances. First, we redesign the merging mechanism to enable frequent interaction between left and right contexts, substantially improving predictive performance over prior hollow transformers. Second, we derive a lower-variance estimator of the MDM NELBO that supervises all tokens and improves validation perplexity. Together, these advances yield a competitive standalone diffusion language model capable of effective self-correction during inference. On LM1B, LOOT matches the strongest dense-supervision MDM baseline in validation perplexity. On OpenWebText, LOOT achieves higher MAUVE and better generation quality-diversity tradeoffs than prior remasking methods, using $8\times$ fewer forward evaluations and $3.5\times$ fewer inference FLOPs.

title: The CYBER-BRIDGE project: An AI-Powered Platform for Cross-Border Cybersecurity, Compliance and Forensics in the EU
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Confer Resilience (IEEE CSR 2026)
summary: Cross-border cyber attacks on European SMEs and critical-infrastructure operators expose a structural cyber-resilience gap: cybersecurity (threat sharing, detection, response), compliance (framework assessment, certification) and digital forensics (cross-jurisdictional evidence) are jointly regulated by NIS2, the CRA, GDPR and the LED, yet their tooling evolved in silos and rarely interoperates across Member States. The EU-funded CYBER-BRIDGE project integrates the three domains under one architecture and a hash-chained evidence layer: AI-driven CTI sharing with ENISA-aligned notification, multi-framework assessments with retrieval-augmented advisory, and RFC 3161-anchored custody with lawful GDPR/LED exchange, all aligned with MITRE ATT&CK. A sanitised replica of the back-end image hosts a Cyber-Range for upskilling. The contribution is not the individual tools but the reconciliation mechanism that lets one incident produce, from a single evidence record, a cross-border CTI advisory, the regulatory notifications its deadlines demand and a re-verifiable forensic pack; we set out why binding three differently regulated evidence regimes onto one record is non-trivial and how the shared evidence layer resolves the resulting tensions. This paper introduces the project's scope, requirements, pilots, architecture and toolkits; quantitative KPIs follow in later deliverables.

title: Physics-Informed Direct Data-Driven Gain-Scheduled Control for Improving the Extrapolation Performance of Vehicle Lateral Control
summary: This paper proposes a physics-informed direct data-driven control (PI-D3C) framework for designing a gain-scheduled proportional-integral controller for vehicle yaw-rate tracking. Vehicle lateral dynamics vary depending on vehicle velocity, making it difficult for controllers designed using data collected over a limited operating range to maintain satisfactory control performance outside that range. We introduce a novel PI-D3C framework that integrates pure data-driven virtual reference feedback tuning (VRFT) with prior physical knowledge, thereby significantly improving extrapolation performance beyond the operating range covered by the collected data. In the proposed approach, the gain-scheduled controller parameters are designed based on both training data and the yaw-rate response predicted by the physics-based model. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed method, numerical simulations are conducted using co-simulation between MATLAB/Simulink and CarSim. The results demonstrate that the controller designed by pure VRFT achieves satisfactory tracking performance within the training velocity region but exhibits significant deterioration in tracking performance outside the training region. In contrast, the proposed controller maintains good yaw-rate tracking performance over a wider velocity range while suppressing excessive variations in the scheduled gains and steering input. These results indicate that incorporating prior physical knowledge into pure data-driven VRFT improves the extrapolation performance of gain-scheduled controllers designed using limited training data.

title: How Much Determinism Can Fine-Tuning Buy? Margin Regularisation Against Batch-Induced Token Flips
summary: Greedy decoding at zero temperature is widely assumed to be deterministic, although the exact same prompt may yield different tokens depending on the number of other prompts sharing the batch for inference. The currently available solutions operate during inference, trading determinism for throughput. Can we train a model in such a way that fewer decoding steps would be susceptible? We characterize the perturbation empirically across six model families and three numerical precisions and observe two empirical facts about the measurement: the perturbation depends exactly on the representable precision (8.00x for bfloat16 vs float16, 8192.0x for float16 vs float32, in line with predictions based on mantissa bits) and the batch invariance happens accidentally at certain tensor shapes, allowing a practitioner to achieve zero nondeterminism merely by setting the sequence length. Then we apply hinge penalization of the model's top-1 / top-2 logit gap, scaled to twice the measured noise quantile. On GSM8K dataset it leads to a 35% reduction in token flips and divergence from 53.8% to 38.1%, at the cost of 1.3 - 2.9 accuracy points, increasing monotonically with the margin size. It does not affect the gap threshold sufficient for determinism: the logit gaps of surviving flips are unchanged (median 0.125 for all arms), as the hinge is a soft penalty and the largest hardware perturbation remains the same. We reject seven hypotheses, including a per-model viability diagnosis, holding on six models and falsified on the seventh.

title: A Rollout-Based Approach to Real-Time Topology and Dispatch Control in the AI4RealNet L2RPN Benchmark
summary: Operating transmission networks under uncertain outages requires coordinating discrete network topology actions with continuous adjustments to generation and storage, while respecting operational constraints and real-time computational limits. We present a rollout-based controller that combines discrete and continuous decisions under the uncertain contingency policy of the L2RPN AI4RealNet 2026 challenge. Power-flow approximations and convex optimization identify the most promising actions, followed by short-horizon simulations to predict their effect on congestion, renewable curtailment, and redispatching costs. A further policy exploits the benchmark's specific attack protocol: keeping selected lines disconnected prevents some adversarial outages from being initiated. On the benchmark's $118$-bus network, the controller completed $189$ of $208$ final-test scenarios (score $64.39$) and achieved the second-best ratio of score to computation time among the five top-ranked entries, behind one that scored lower. Our results show that combining structured optimization with simulation-based action selection is effective even without a learned decision rule, and fast enough for real-time control. Code and reproduction material: https://github.com/DavidKrame/RAD_agent__AI4RealNet_competition.

title: LogT: Logically Think with Images for Visual Search
summary: Thinking with images empowers vision-language models (VLMs) to use an external Zoom-in tool for fine-grained visual search. Recent works employ supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) with tool-specific designs to enable such capabilities. However, achieving logical reasoning alongside accurate and efficient tool use remains a significant challenge. To address this, we shift the focus away from increasing RL complexity and instead identify SFT data quality as a key bottleneck. We then propose LogT (short for Logically Think with Images), a fully automated SFT data engine that explicitly enforces logic-chain-guided reasoning. LogT generates an SFT dataset featuring challenging, visually grounded questions and structured tool-use traces with human-like logic. We validate our approach by fine-tuning two base models, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3.5-8B, on the dataset and evaluating them across seven benchmark test sets. We show that LogT-SFT based on Qwen2.5-VL-7B outperforms the state-of-the-art trained with both SFT and RL, despite using 3.1$\times$ less data and $>120\times$ fewer GPU hours. Furthermore, applying a simple RL recipe without tool-specific design on LogT-SFT yields a model that surpasses prior methods with complex RL setups by a substantial 9.59-point margin. In addition to strong performance gains, our model exhibits higher tool-use accuracy and efficiency, as well as more structured and logically consistent reasoning traces, directly validating the effectiveness of our approach.

title: TRACE: Topological Representations for Anomaly detection through Contrastive Embeddings
summary: Intrusion detectors must recognize evolving malicious behavior even when confirmed attack labels are scarce or incomplete. We present TRACE, a topology-aware graph contrastive learning framework for label-efficient intrusion detection. TRACE learns from benign system-activity graphs by combining message-passing and topological representations, then assigns anomaly scores in the same projected embedding space optimized by the contrastive objective.
